metaData.originalTitle: 3 Agents. 3 LLMs. 1 Aging GPU: Engineering Parallel Inference on Bare Metal
metaData.title: 3 Agents. 3 LLMs. 1 Aging GPU: Engineering Parallel Inference on Bare Metal
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article explains why running multiple LLM-based agents in parallel on a single low-VRAM GPU fails due to KV cache pre-allocation, and presents a small C++ daemon (lmxd) that enforces VRAM bookkeeping to solve the problem.
metaData.summary: The article addresses the practical challenge of running three AI agents, each using a different small LLM, on a single GTX 1080 with only 8 GB VRAM. The naive approach of launching separate llama-completion processes fails because each process pre-reserves a large KV cache for the full context window, causing the second and third processes to OOM. The author introduces lmxd, a ~1500-line C++ daemon that acts as a VRAM bookkeeper. Agents communicate with the daemon over a Unix socket using a simple text protocol (REGISTER, DECODE, etc.). The daemon maintains a ledger that enforces a 90% VRAM cap, admits new agents only if the estimated memory fits, and loads models in a shared backend to avoid redundant CUDA context overhead. The article provides detailed code snippets, explains the critical order of operations (book before build), and presents benchmark results on the same hardware, showing that the daemon successfully admits all three agents where the naive approach admits only one. It also covers KV-swap mechanisms for time-slicing decode across agents, and draws an insightful analogy to Connection Admission Control (CAC) in cellular networks.

mainPoints.point: Multiple llama-completion processes fail in parallel due to upfront KV cache pre-allocation, not model weights.
mainPoints.explanation: Each process reserves VRAM for the full context window (e.g., 6.5 GB for Llama 1B with large context), leaving insufficient space for other processes. The OOM is caused by KV cache reservation, not the model itself.

mainPoints.point: A VRAM ledger with simple admission control solves the overcommitment problem.
mainPoints.explanation: The daemon maintains a ledger of allocated bytes and admits a new agent only if current usage plus estimated need stays under a configurable cap (e.g., 90%). This prevents OOM at registration time.

mainPoints.point: The order of operations matters: book (reserve in ledger) before build (load model).
mainPoints.explanation: If you load the model first and check budget second, you waste I/O and risk races. The daemon reserves VRAM in the ledger before any GGUF is loaded, and rolls back on failure, leaving no trace.

mainPoints.point: Sharing a single llama backend avoids redundant CUDA context overhead.
mainPoints.explanation: By initializing llama_backend once and sharing a refcounted model map, the daemon reuses weights and avoids hundreds of megabytes of per-process driver overhead.

mainPoints.point: The problem mirrors Connection Admission Control (CAC) in cellular networks.
mainPoints.explanation: Just as a base station decides whether to admit a new call without degrading existing ones, the daemon rejects new agents before they load if they would exceed VRAM capacity, with clear error codes.

keyQuotes: The fix is not 'a better algorithm.' It is the simplest of all: bookkeeping.
Failure that explains itself is the most beautiful thing.
Same animal in a new zoo.

relatedArticles.title: Stop Treating AI Memory Like a Search Problem
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article critiques the conventional 'store-and-retrieve' approach to AI memory, proposing a lifecycle-based system with decay, contradiction detection, confidence scoring, compression, and expiry to manage memory like a human brain rather than a static archive.

relatedArticles.title: Codex and Subagents — Vaibhav Srivastav & Katia Gil Guzman， OpenAI
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI developers walk through Codex's full engineering platform—subagents for parallel execution, a plugin ecosystem, background automations, Guardian safety gates, and MCP integrations—showing why it has reached 3 million weekly active users.

relatedArticles.title: State of the Claw
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenClaw founder and OpenAI engineer Peter Steinberger discusses the unprecedented growth and security challenges of the OpenClaw project, shares his unique AI-assisted development workflow, and explores the evolving concept of 'engineer taste' in the AI era.

relatedArticles.title: Embeddings Aren’t Magic: The Predictable Failure Modes of RAG Retrieval
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically debunks the magic of embeddings in RAG systems, demonstrating through reproducible experiments that embeddings excel at public vocabulary tasks but predictably fail on enterprise-specific terms, negation, magnitudes, and answer relevance, advocating for upstream filtering over stronger models.

relatedArticles.title: How OpenAI delivers low-latency voice AI at scale
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI rearchitected its WebRTC stack using a split relay and transceiver model to deliver low-latency voice AI at scale, solving port exhaustion and state stickiness in Kubernetes.

relatedArticles.title: Your ReAct Agent Is Wasting 90% of Its Retries — Here’s How to Stop It
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article identifies a critical architectural flaw in ReAct-style LLM agents where hallucinated tool names waste the majority of retry budgets, and proposes three structural fixes—error taxonomy, per-tool circuit breakers, and deterministic tool routing—to eliminate this waste and improve production reliability.

relatedArticles.title: Building an Evaluation Harness for Production AI Agents: A 12-Metric Framework From 100+ Deployments
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article presents a comprehensive 12-metric evaluation framework for production AI agents, distilled from over 100 enterprise deployments, covering retrieval, generation, agent behavior, and production health.

relatedArticles.title: Harness Engineering: How to Build Software When Humans Steer, Agents Execute
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI engineer Ryan Lopopolo introduces 'Harness Engineering,' a paradigm shift where engineers design systems and automated guardrails to orchestrate hundreds of AI agents, transforming from coders to directors of software development.

relatedArticles.title: Hybrid Search and Re-Ranking in Production RAG
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article presents a production-grade approach to improving RAG retrieval quality by combining hybrid search (BM25 + dense vectors) with cross-encoder re-ranking and metadata filtering, supported by real-world evaluation metrics.

relatedArticles.title: Memory and Dreaming for Self-Learning Agents
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Anthropic introduces Memory and Dreaming, two new primitives for its Managed Agents API, enabling agents to achieve continuous self-learning by managing their own knowledge in a file system-like structure and asynchronously curating that knowledge to improve over time.
